extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of poetics, poets, literary critics and creative-writing practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines drawn from Aristotelian poetics about what makes effective poetry and fine art: emphasis on expressing the universal rather than the particular, internal probability/necessity, the artist's shaping activity, the permissible scope of fiction and the marvelous, and distinctions between epic and dramatic treatments. Useful for evaluating or producing poems, dramas, and epic narrative with respect to classical aesthetic principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine art as completion or idealization of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine art 'presents to us only an image, but a purified image of nature’s original.' It reveals the ideal form at which nature aims by removing flaws and failures incident to natural processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The artist 'ignores the intervening steps' and embodies the ideal in a finished product; fine art does not seek to modify the actual world but, by imagery, discloses the ideal that nature strives toward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between useful art and fine art
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful art employs nature's machinery to serve practical needs; fine art sets practical needs aside and aims to reveal the ideal rather than to effect material change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful art furthers nature's purpose in practicality; fine art is a completion of nature in a non-practical sense and is judged by its revelation of the ideal rather than utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry expresses the universal (τὰ καθόλου) not the particular
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinguishing mark of poetry is that it 'expresses most adequately the universal element in human nature and in life' and 'relates what may happen' rather than merely 'what has happened.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry abstracts from accidental particulars and represents 'what may happen' according to the law of probability or necessity; this is the higher subject-matter that differentiates poetry from history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on internal causal connexion, probability and necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should exhibit a more rigorous connexion of events and internal order than ordinary experience: events must cohere by 'probability' (εἰκός) or 'necessity' (ἀναγκαῖον) in the internal structure of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule of probability in art is not a statistical average of everyday occurrence but an inner law securing cohesion; improbable events in real life may be acceptable if internally probable within the poem’s logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth as 'what ought to be' (higher reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may represent things that 'never have happened' yet be 'a higher reality' — 'what ought to be (ὡς δεῖ),' giving the form that answers to the true idea rather than mere empirical fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet's creations can be 'unreal' relative to fact but 'better' or truer in revealing the universal; evaluate poetry by its fidelity to the ideal or universal rather than by factual historicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish errors of poetic essence from factual inaccuracies
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a difference between errors affecting the essence of poetic art and incidental factual errors in relation to other arts; minor oversights are not fatal if the total impression remains unimpaired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor technical or factual mistakes may be tolerated provided they do not damage the poem's essential artistic effect; the crucial test is whether the total impression and internal principles of the work are preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible poetic invention (the art of feigning) provided internal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may make primary assumptions ('πρῶτον ψεῦδος') and invent impossible or marvellous elements, so long as starting from those poetic data the sequence of incident and motive makes the events happen 'exactly as they would have happened' had the fiction been fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vividness, minuteness of detail and natural sequence to make original falsehoods plausible; 'probable impossibilities' are to be preferred to 'improbable possibilities.' The inner consistency and plausibility within the fictional frame are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrational elements (ἄλογα) are especially suspect and need justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that are 'irrational'—that offend reason rather than merely defy empirical fact—are greater stumbling-blocks to poetic acceptance and require special justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such elements may be admitted if they produce heightened wonder/admiration (especially in epic) or if they rest on tradition/popular belief; but they are less admissible in drama, where irrationality provokes critical hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional legends and popular belief as permissible material
rubrics_metrics.description: Marvellous or supernatural facts enshrined in current tradition or belief may be proper material for poetry; they are 'ἀδύνατα' of experience but not necessarily 'ἄλογα' of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If marvellous elements form coherent shape within a people's mythology and express underlying convictions, poets may incorporate them; poets can sometimes harmonise natural and supernatural into a rational-imaginative order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-sensitivity: epic vs drama suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain incidents (marvellous or improbable) may be acceptable in epic narrative but inappropriate on the stage; epic distance can sustain illusions that drama's immediate presentation would expose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate incidents by medium — e.g., Achilles chasing Hector round Troy's walls works as epic narrative (producing wonder) but would seem ludicrous if presented directly in dramatic performance; choose treatment consistent with medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist's shaping activity: purification and selection of material
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's creative task is to extract the 'ore' from historical or legendary material, to free it from the accidental and irrelevant, and to idealise and combine parts into a unified, poetic structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even 'founded on fact' tragedies must transmute fact into imaginative truth by purification and shaping; the artist's structuring and selection determine poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be idealized, fully human, and not mere averages
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic characters are typically not 'average men' but persons capable of great deeds and passions; they must be represented with full humanity so readers can enlarge their sympathies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not evaluate characters by frequency in actual life; instead ensure their actions and emotions are internally coherent and evoke sympathetic enlargement in the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as a regulative principle but not the sole end of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle treats beauty as indispensable and essential to art's end yet does not analyze it as a separate domain; objective laws of art are deduced from observation of art and its effects rather than from an abstract theory of the beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While beauty should be present and serve as a regulative guide, evaluations should focus on the objective laws and effects (e.g., unity, probability, catharsis) observed in successful works rather than an a priori definition of beauty.
